quests.instruction: When a rower pulls the oars backwards, what do the oars push against to move the boat forward?
quests.hint: The blades of the oars are underneath the surface.
quests.explanation: Oars push water backwards, and the water pushes the boat forward. Every push needs something to push against.
quests.funFact: Racing rowing boats are long and narrow so they slip through the water easily.

quests.instruction: What do a car's tyres grip to push the car forward?
quests.hint: Without it, the wheels would just spin.
quests.explanation: Wheels push backwards against the road, and the grip pushes the vehicle forward. On slippery ground, wheels can spin without moving.
quests.funFact: Tractors and bulldozers sometimes use tracks instead of wheels to spread their weight and grip soft ground.

quests.instruction: What does an airplane's propeller push backwards to move the plane forward?
quests.hint: It is invisible but all around the plane.
quests.explanation: A propeller spins and pushes air backwards. The air pushes the plane forward.
quests.funFact: Some propellers on large planes are taller than a person.

quests.instruction: Which toothed wheel lets a bike rider switch to an easier setting for climbing hills?
quests.hint: The chain fits around its teeth.
quests.explanation: Gears change how far the wheel turns for each turn of the pedals. A low gear makes hills easier, while a high gear helps you go fast on flat ground.
quests.funFact: Some modern road bikes have more than twenty gear settings.

quests.instruction: What do petrol and diesel engines burn to make the energy that moves a vehicle?
quests.hint: It is stored in a tank.
quests.explanation: An engine burns fuel mixed with air, which releases energy. That energy turns the wheels.
quests.funFact: Petrol and diesel are made from crude oil.

quests.instruction: What leaves the back of many engines after fuel has been burned?
quests.hint: It comes out of a pipe at the back.
quests.explanation: Burning fuel makes waste gases, called exhaust. They leave through the exhaust pipe and can make the air dirty.
quests.funFact: Electric vehicles have no exhaust pipe.

quests.instruction: A cyclist squeezes the brake levers. What happens to the bicycle?
quests.hint: Squeezing makes something rub against the wheel.
quests.explanation: Brakes use friction to slow the wheels. The harder you squeeze, the more the bicycle slows.
quests.funFact: Bicycle brakes rub rubber pads against the wheel rim or a metal disc.

quests.instruction: Which of these gives tyres the least grip?
quests.hint: It is cold, hard, and very slippery.
quests.explanation: Ice is very slippery, so tyres cannot grip well. Drivers slow down and leave extra space on icy roads.
quests.funFact: Some winter tyres have tiny metal studs that bite into the ice.

quests.instruction: A loaded train takes a long distance to stop mainly because it is so what?
quests.hint: Think about how hard it is to stop a very heavy trolley.
quests.explanation: Heavy things are hard to stop. Long trains with heavy loads can need hundreds of metres to come to a halt.
quests.funFact: A fully loaded freight train can need more than a kilometre to stop.

quests.instruction: A driver wants to turn right at the next corner. Which arrow does the indicator show?
quests.hint: It points toward the right-hand side of the screen.
quests.explanation: Indicators warn other road users which way a vehicle will turn. Using them early helps everyone predict what you will do.
quests.funFact: Indicators flash on and off so they are easier to notice.

quests.instruction: A cyclist holds out an arm to show a turn to the left. Which hand signal points left?
quests.hint: The pointing finger shows the side of the road they plan to move toward.
quests.explanation: Hand signals tell other road users what you plan to do. Cyclists should look behind and signal early before turning.
quests.funFact: Hand signals were used long before cars had indicators.

quests.instruction: Which arrow shows a U-turn, where a driver goes back the way they came?
quests.hint: The arrow curves round and heads back.
quests.explanation: A U-turn turns the vehicle around to face the opposite direction. It is only safe where it is allowed and the road is clear.
quests.funFact: Some roads have signs that forbid U-turns.

quests.instruction: What invisible pull holds everything down to the ground and must be overcome for a plane to rise?
quests.hint: It is why things fall when you drop them.
quests.explanation: Earth's gravity pulls everything toward it. Wings, engines, or rockets must push upward harder than gravity pulls down.
quests.funFact: Gravity is weaker on the Moon, so astronauts can bounce along there.

quests.instruction: Which device bounces radio waves off objects to find planes and ships, even in fog or darkness?
quests.hint: Picture a dish that sends and receives signals.
quests.explanation: Radar sends out radio waves and listens for echoes. It shows air traffic controllers and ship captains where other vehicles are.
quests.funFact: Weather forecasters also use radar to track rain.

quests.instruction: What shoots out of the bottom of a rocket as it lifts off?
quests.hint: It is very hot and very bright.
quests.explanation: A rocket burns fuel and blasts hot gas downward. The gas is pushed down, so the rocket is pushed up.
quests.funFact: Rocket engines can reach temperatures of thousands of degrees.

quests.instruction: To move a very heavy box across a smooth floor, which helps the most?
quests.hint: It rolls.
quests.explanation: Rolling takes much less effort than sliding. That is why trolleys, carts, and trucks have wheels.
quests.funFact: Builders have long used rolling logs to help move heavy loads.

quests.instruction: Which place has long downhill slopes where a cyclist can coast without pedalling?
quests.hint: Gravity does the work on the way down.
quests.explanation: On a downhill slope, gravity pulls the cyclist and bicycle along. Riders can coast and keep their feet resting on the pedals.
quests.funFact: Some mountain roads are famous for long downhill rides.

quests.instruction: What pushes against a fast cyclist's face and body, slowing them down?
quests.hint: You cannot see it, but you can feel it, especially when you go fast.
quests.explanation: Air pushes back against moving things. Riders crouch low to reduce this push, which is called air resistance.
quests.funFact: Racing cyclists ride in groups and take turns at the front, because the leader faces the most wind.

quests.instruction: Which dashboard warning shows that a car's engine is getting too hot?
quests.hint: It looks like a measuring tool for heat.
quests.explanation: Engines make heat, and cooling liquid carries it away. If an engine overheats, the driver should stop safely and let it cool.
quests.funFact: Many cars use red for urgent warnings and amber for things to check soon.

quests.instruction: Which dashboard symbol warns that a door might not be closed properly?
quests.hint: It looks like a panel that swings open.
quests.explanation: An open or loose door can fall open or let in cold air. The warning tells the driver to check before moving.
quests.funFact: Some cars beep if a door is open while the vehicle is moving.

quests.instruction: Which dashboard symbol warns of an electrical charging problem?
quests.hint: It looks like something that stores electricity.
quests.explanation: A car's battery needs to be kept charged while the engine runs. A warning means the electrical system needs checking.
quests.funFact: A car's electrical system also powers its lights, radio, and windows.

quests.instruction: Which safety feature inflates in a crash to cushion the people inside a car?
quests.hint: It blows up in a fraction of a second.
quests.explanation: An airbag fills with gas in a split second to soften the impact. It works together with seat belts, never instead of them.
quests.funFact: An airbag inflates in less than a tenth of a second.

quests.instruction: What small red piece at the back of a bicycle bounces back headlight beams so drivers can see it?
quests.hint: It does not make light, but it sends light back.
quests.explanation: A reflector sends light straight back to where it came from. Drivers see the glow and know a bicycle is there.
quests.funFact: Reflectors work without batteries.

quests.instruction: When a car breaks down on the road, which lights flash to warn other drivers?
quests.hint: They flash on both sides at once.
quests.explanation: Hazard lights warn others of danger. They help prevent collisions when a vehicle is stopped or moving slowly.
quests.funFact: Hazard lights are often turned on with a button marked with a red triangle.

quests.instruction: Which signal keeps two trains from using the same piece of track at the same time?
quests.hint: It uses coloured lights, like on a road.
quests.explanation: Railway signals tell drivers whether the track ahead is clear. Tracks are divided into sections, and only one train is allowed in a section at a time.
quests.funFact: Different countries use different signal patterns on their railways.

quests.instruction: At a railway crossing, a red light flashes and the barriers come down. What must drivers do?
quests.hint: Never try to beat the train.
quests.explanation: A train cannot stop quickly or swerve, so drivers must wait until the barriers rise and the lights stop flashing.
quests.funFact: Many railway crossings have bells or lights to warn people that a train is near.

quests.instruction: Which colour usually tells a train driver the way ahead is clear?
quests.hint: It is the same colour that means go on a road traffic light.
quests.explanation: Green usually means the line ahead is clear. Yellow means be ready to stop, and red means stop.
quests.funFact: Railway signals were once worked by moving arms before coloured lights became common.

quests.instruction: Which invisible force lets some very fast trains float just above their track?
quests.hint: Think of what pulls a fridge door shut.
quests.explanation: Maglev trains use powerful magnets to lift and push the train. With no wheels touching the track, there is almost no friction.
quests.funFact: Shanghai in China has a maglev train that links an airport with the city.

quests.instruction: Which part helps a self-driving car see the road, lane markings, and other cars?
quests.hint: It takes pictures all the time.
quests.explanation: Self-driving cars use cameras and other sensors to see around them. A computer uses what they see to make driving decisions.
quests.funFact: Many modern cars use cameras to help with parking and staying in lane.

quests.instruction: Which liquid helps the moving parts of an engine slide smoothly instead of grinding?
quests.hint: It is slippery, dark, and golden-brown.
quests.explanation: Engine oil coats moving parts so they rub less. Without it, an engine would overheat and wear out.
quests.funFact: Cars have a small stick called a dipstick for checking the oil level.
